WHO launches framework to protect mothers and babies from extreme heat
The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a framework with the first set of priority indicators to track extreme heat risks for pregnant women, newborns and children.
The indicators are intended to help countries monitor heat-related health impacts, improve preparedness and respond more quickly to rising temperatures.
The launch follows growing evidence linking extreme heat exposure to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including a 26 per cent increase in the odds of preterm birth.
Dr Pascale Allotey, director of WHO’s Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing, said: “Heat is already affecting our most vulnerable populations, including pregnant women, newborns and children.
“But what health systems do not count, they cannot respond to.
“By tracking outcomes such as preterm birth, child deaths and illnesses, and health-facility visits alongside heat exposure, countries can identify potential impacts and take action to protect women and children.”
WHO developed the framework with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), UNICEF and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).
The organisations say it will help health authorities monitor risks among populations particularly vulnerable to extreme heat.
Research cited in the announcement found that babies under one year of age experienced 389 per cent more days of heatwave exposure in 2024 compared with the 1986 to 2005 baseline period.
The figure refers to the increase in days of exposure to heatwaves, rather than an increase in temperature.
Globally, an estimated 1.5 billion children are exposed to heatwaves that are becoming more frequent, longer or more severe.
The framework recommends monitoring preterm births, stillbirths, low birthweight, pregnancy-related hypertension (high blood pressure), child deaths and visits to healthcare facilities during periods of extreme heat.
School attendance could also be tracked to identify disruption caused by high temperatures.
Combining routine health data with heat-exposure information, including air temperature, could help countries spot unusual changes in health outcomes.
These findings could prompt further investigation and help authorities decide where protective measures are needed.
The information could help health authorities prepare facilities for increased demand, strengthen warnings to pregnant women and families, identify higher-risk communities and improve heat-health planning.
Bruce Gordon, acting director of WHO’s Department of Environment, Climate Change, One Health and Migration, said rising temperatures were creating additional health risks for older people, pregnant women, newborns and children.
He called for greater use of data to guide protective measures and for climate risks to be incorporated into routine healthcare.

title: SA braces for hot, dry weekend as heatwave persists - TimesLIVE

full_text:
South Africans can expect hot and largely dry conditions across much of the country this weekend, with below-normal rainfall forecast in several provinces over the coming weeks, the South African Weather Service (Saws) has warned.
In its sub-seasonal outlook covering October 21 to November 3, Saws said the highest temperatures were expected in Limpopo, Mpumalanga’s Lowveld, parts of the North West and Northern Cape, as well as northern Gauteng.
Below-normal rainfall is forecast across much of the country, particularly in the summer rainfall regions of KwaZulu-Natal, Gauteng, the eastern Free State, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and the North West.
Meteorologist and weather forecaster Lehlohonolo Thobela said the forecast indicated generally hot and dry conditions over much of the central and eastern parts of South Africa.
However, parts of the western interior could experience relatively wetter and cooler conditions as the forecast period progresses. These areas include:
the southern high ground of the Northern Cape;
the Western Cape;
western parts of the Eastern Cape; and
the western and southern parts of the North West and Free State.
“Showers and thunderstorms may develop over these areas as the forecast period progresses,” Thobela said, adding that the distribution and intensity of rainfall would depend on prevailing weather systems.
Saws warned that prolonged periods of high temperatures and below-normal rainfall could place additional pressure on water resources, agriculture and communities that depend on regular rainfall
For this weekend, residents in Gauteng, North West and the Free State can expect generally fine and warm to hot conditions.
In Limpopo, the heatwave affecting parts of the western bushveld is expected to remain a concern. Mpumalanga is forecast to experience partly cloudy conditions in its eastern parts, with isolated light showers and rain possible along the escarpment.
The Northern Cape is expected to remain mostly fine and warm to hot, although cooler conditions are forecast in the extreme south.
KwaZulu-Natal is expected to be cloudy and warm, with isolated showers, while the Eastern Cape is forecast to experience partly cloudy to cloudy and cool conditions.
Saws warned that prolonged periods of high temperatures and below-normal rainfall could place additional pressure on water resources, agriculture and communities that depend on regular rainfall.
Higher temperatures increase evaporation from dams, reservoirs and soil. Combined with reduced rainfall, this could put further pressure on water resources, particularly in areas already experiencing water constraints.
People are urged to check on vulnerable family members and neighbours and remain alert to official heatwave advisories
Farmers could also face reduced soil moisture, increased irrigation requirements and heat stress affecting crops and livestock if the conditions persist.
Thobela said the public should take precautions against excessive heat, particularly vulnerable groups such as young children, older people and those with underlying health conditions.
Residents are encouraged to drink sufficient water, avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight during the hottest part of the day, wear lightweight clothing and take regular breaks when working outdoors.
People are also urged to check on vulnerable family members and neighbours and remain alert to official heatwave advisories.
Saws said sub-seasonal forecasts indicate likely weather patterns over two to four weeks rather than exact daily conditions. While the outlook points to generally above-normal temperatures and below-normal rainfall across much of the country, confidence varies by region and weather parameter.
The public has also been urged to exercise caution in Mahikeng and Ratlou in the North West, where extremely high fire danger conditions have been forecast. Activities that could ignite veld fires should be avoided.

The weather will continue to be intense for Tamil Nadu and Kerala due to the development of yet another low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal, leading to heavy to very heavy rainfall in several regions. Tamil Nadu has been witnessed deep spells of downpour and thunderstorms since past two consecutive days with no sight of relief at least until October 27, 2026. IMD has already issued yellow and orange alerts in dozes of cities in Tamil Nadu. Because of this, as precautionary measure, many districts have declared school holiday on October 23, 2026.
IMD Weather Alert:
As per IMD, under the influence of the low-pressure area over Comorin Area & adjoining South Tamil Nadu and Keralam, isolated heavy to very heavy rainfall likely over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry & Karaikal during 22nd -26th and Keralam during 22nd-25th.
For Tamil Nadu, IMD believes that heavy to very heavy rain at isolated places with thunderstorm & lightning with gusty wind speed reaching 40-50 kmph at one or two places is likely to occur over Kanyakumari, Nilgiris and Coimbatore districts.
Also, heavy rain at isolated places with thunderstorm & lightning with gusty wind speed reaching 40-50 kmph at one or two places is likely to occur over Erode, Salem, Namakkal, Karur, Tiruchirappalli, Tenkasi, Theni, Dindigul, Madurai, Virudhunagar, Pudukkottai, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam, Mayiladuthurai, Sivaganga, Ramanathapuram, Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli, Ariyalur, Cuddalore, Villuppuram, Tiruppur, Perambalur, Chennai, Tiruvallur districts, Puducherry and Karaikal area.
Meanwhile, moderate rain at many places with thunderstorms & lightning with gusty wind speeds reaching 40-50 kmph at one or two places is likely to occur over the rest of Tamil Nadu.
Meanwhile, the rest of the region will see moderate rains with 40-50 kmph gusty winds.
Tamil Nadu Weather: IMD Issues Orange, Yellow Alerts
Accordingly, IMD has issued Orange Alerts at isolated places over Kanyakumari, Coimbatore, Nilgiris and Ghat areas of Tirunelveli districts.
Further, for October 23, due to heavy rains, IMD issued Yellow Alerts at isolated places over Erode, Salem, Namakkal, Karur, Tiruchirappalli, Tenkasi, Theni, Dindigul, Madurai, Virudhunagar, Pudukkottai, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam, Mayiladuthurai, Sivaganga, Ramanathapuram, Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli, Ariyalur, Cuddalore, Villuppuram, Tiruppur, Perambalur, Chennai, Tiruvallur districts, Puducherry and Karaikal area.
Tamil Nadu Weather: Are Schools Closed Today?
As per reports, the respective District Collectors have declared school holidays in regions of Tiruvannamalai, Villupuram and Kallakurichi on October 23, 2026. Notably, in Tiruvannamalai, both schools and colleges are declared to be shut due to the weather on Thursday, but in Villupuram and Kallakurichi, only schools will remain closed.
On the other hand, Chengalpattu and Kancheepuram District Collectors stated that schools and colleges in these two districts will remain open as normal.
Yesterday, Chennai joined other districts to declare school holidays on October 22nd as incessant rains took a toll over the city. However, no new official statement regarding schools being closed on October 23 in Chennai. Accordingly, it is advisable to check with local authorities or school administration on whether schools are open or closed in the city.

France issues orange alert in 15 departments ahead of Storm Austen — Anadolu Agency
France has issued an orange weather alert in 15 departments in the western and northern parts of the country ahead of Storm Austen. Wind gusts are forecast to reach 140 kilometers per hour.
Warning for the Atlantic coast
France’s national meteorological service, Météo-France, warned that the powerful storm will primarily affect the Atlantic coast. Anadolu Agency reports on the alert.
The departments under the orange alert include Loire-Atlantique, Nord, Pas-de-Calais, Somme, Yvelines, Finistère and Val-d’Oise. The source does not provide a full list of all 15 departments.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Wind will spread inland
Strong winds are expected to spread to inland areas of France over the weekend. They may also affect the Île-de-France region, which includes Paris.
Storm Austen is forecast to bring heavy rainfall, primarily to Brittany and Normandy.
